topic: Setting a closure rule for a coastal path
grammarFocus: 学术论证的限定、因果、对比与证据范围
title: Setting a closure rule for a coastal path
instructions: 原创学术微训练；场景、机构与数值均为虚构模拟，不是事实报道或官方试题。先独立阅读答题，再用原句核对限定、比较与因果。短篇专项不能替代完整陌生测评。
passage:
A. A simulated coastal authority managed a path beneath a low cliff. After several storms, staff proposed closing the route whenever the water reached a marked post. The post was easy for walkers to recognise, and a simple rule could be communicated quickly. Yet the engineers cautioned that one visible marker would not describe every source of danger along the path.

B. Water level mattered most near the harbour entrance. Further along the route, loose stones could fall even when the tide was low. A threshold designed for flooding would not automatically protect walkers from falling material. The authority therefore separated the flood warning from the cliff inspection. Closing one section did not imply that every other section was safe; each had its own conditions for reopening.

C. Residents disagreed about how often the path should close. Shop owners worried that frequent closures would discourage visitors. A walking group preferred a cautious rule because alternative access was available inland. Both positions involved a judgement about acceptable risk, not merely a disagreement over measured water levels. The authority published the reasons for its provisional rule instead of presenting the marker as a scientific guarantee.

D. To review the decision, staff recorded closure times, inspection findings and reports of water crossing the path. The absence of an accident during a closed period would not prove that closure was unnecessary: people had been kept away from the possible hazard. Equally, a few uneventful open days could not establish that the risk was permanently negligible.

E. The first review was scheduled after the winter season. It would examine whether warning signs were visible and whether visitors understood the inland diversion. This practical information could improve the policy even if it did not resolve every uncertainty about future storms. The aim was to make a defensible decision under incomplete information, then revise it openly as evidence accumulated. The authority retained earlier versions of the rule so that later changes could be traced.
